content: Hot flushes, also referred to as hot flashes, are the most common symptom experienced during menopause. Menopause, or the climacteric phase, encompasses the physiological and pathological changes that occur due to reduced ovarian function, both before and after the final menstrual period. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), hot flushes are characterized by a sudden sensation of heat, typically affecting the face, neck, and chest. These episodes can vary in severity and frequency, occurring during the day or night. When they occur at night, they are often referred to as night sweats. Together, hot flushes and night sweats are the hallmark symptoms of vasomotor menopausal changes. The exact cause of hot flushes remains complex and not fully understood. However, it is believed to result from instability in the thermoregulatory center of the hypothalamus, triggered by the withdrawal of estrogen and progesterone. External factors, such as stress or anxiety, may exacerbate these symptoms by influencing neuroendocrine pathways, leading to increased hypothalamic norepinephrine and serotonin release. This thermoregulatory instability causes sudden, transient, and unpredictable peripheral vasodilation in the skin's blood vessels, accompanied by a sensation of flushing and a measurable rise in core body temperature. Cultural differences in the prevalence of hot flushes have been observed. For instance, Maya Indian women report no menopausal symptoms, while prevalence rates range from 10-22% in Hong Kong women, 17% in Japanese women, 23% in Thai women, 45% in North American women, and up to 80% in Dutch women. Western populations generally report higher rates of hot flushes compared to other regions. Among women who experience hot flushes, the prevalence peaks during the early to late perimenopausal period, defined as 3 to 11 months without menstruation. These symptoms are most common in the first two years after menopause and typically diminish over time, although 10-20% of women may continue to experience them even 15 years post-menopause. Hot flushes are the most frequent physical complaint among women seeking medical assistance for menopausal symptoms, affecting approximately 80% of this population. A longitudinal study in Sweden spanning 25 years revealed that, in the late 1960s, non-hormonal treatments such as antidepressants, sedatives, and anticholinergic drugs were commonly used for hot flushes, with less than 50% of women finding these treatments effective. The use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) increased significantly in the 1980s, with up to 87% of women reporting its effectiveness in alleviating hot flushes. The North American Menopause Society (NAMS) has published guidelines for managing vasomotor symptoms of menopause, categorizing treatment options and evaluating the quality of evidence supporting their use. Lifestyle modifications, such as maintaining a lower core body temperature, losing excess weight, and quitting smoking, may help alleviate mild hot flushes, although these recommendations are based on observational studies rather than randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Relaxation techniques performed at the onset of a hot flush have shown some efficacy in RCTs. Non-prescription remedies include those with hormonal properties, such as isoflavones and topical progesterone, and others with inconclusive evidence of estrogenic effects, such as black cohosh, dong quai, ginseng, and licorice. Interventions without known hormonal effects, such as vitamin E, acupuncture, and magnet therapy, have also been explored. However, evidence regarding the efficacy and long-term safety of these remedies is generally lacking. RCTs have demonstrated that soy-derived isoflavones and vitamin E provide only slight reductions in hot flushes compared to placebo. Topical progesterone, black cohosh, dong quai, ginseng, Chinese herbal mixtures, and magnet therapy have shown no benefit over placebo in RCTs. There is no clinical data from RCTs supporting the efficacy of acupuncture or licorice. Hormonal therapies, particularly HRT with estrogen or estrogen-progesterone combinations, have been shown to be highly effective in reducing the frequency and severity of hot flushes, with a 77% reduction in frequency and significant severity reduction compared to placebo. Progestins alone have also been effective in relieving menopause-associated hot flushes. Oral contraceptives have been evaluated in perimenopausal women, with mixed results. Evidence supporting androgen-estrogen therapy for hot flushes is lacking. Non-hormonal prescription therapies include certain antidepressants, such as venlafaxine, paroxetine, and fluoxetine, which may reduce hot flushes by modulating central serotonin or norepinephrine levels. Gabapentin, an anticonvulsant, has been studied in one RCT, although its mechanism of action in hot flushes is unclear. Antihypertensives, such as clonidine and methyldopa, have been evaluated in RCTs, with clonidine showing more side effects than placebo and methyldopa providing modest symptom reduction. Bellergal spacetab, a combination of low-dose phenobarbital, ergotamine tartrate, and belladonna alkaloids, has been assessed in two RCTs. Tibolone, a synthetic hormone with estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic effects, has been shown in one RCT to be as effective as estrogen-progesterone combinations in relieving hot flushes and other menopausal symptoms. Veralipride, a benzamide derivative with antidopaminergic effects, has been evaluated in two RCTs as a non-hormonal therapy. HRT remains the standard therapy for hot flushes, but data from the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) and the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study (HERS) have linked HRT to increased risks of breast cancer, cardiovascular events, thromboembolism, stroke, and dementia. The risk of breast cancer is higher with prolonged use of estrogen, and even greater with combined estrogen-progesterone therapy beyond five years. These findings have led many women to avoid or discontinue HRT. Contraindications to HRT include confirmed cardiovascular disease, a history of blood-clotting disorders, venous thromboembolism, or hormone-sensitive cancers. For women who cannot or choose not to use HRT, non-hormonal therapies may be appropriate. However, these therapies must be rigorously evaluated in blinded trials against placebo or standard treatments, as the placebo effect is notably high, reaching 51% in well-designed trials for HRT. Trials should also employ validated instruments to accurately measure symptoms. The goal of ongoing research is to determine the effectiveness of non-hormonal pharmacological therapies in alleviating hot flushes during late perimenopause and postmenopause.
